source: docs/RESEARCH.md §b4 (state charity-care laws with mandated thresholds), fetched 2026-10-01

WA.summary: Washington hospitals must give free care up to at least 200% of the poverty line; large systems (Tier A) must go further — free to 300% and discounts to 400%. Applies to the patient-responsibility portion, so insured patients' balances count too.
WA.who: All patients and their guarantors, including the patient-responsibility portion for insured patients.
WA.hospitalsCovered: All WA acute-care hospitals. Tier A = hospitals in 3+ hospital systems, or large hospitals in populous counties. Tier B = everyone else.
caveats: Ask which tier your hospital is in: Tier A (large multi-hospital systems or certain large hospitals) is free ≤300% FPL with discounts to 400%; Tier B (most hospitals) is free ≤200% FPL with discounts to 300%.
WAC 246-453-040 still shows older, lower numbers (free ≤100%); the RCW thresholds above are the current law and override it.
Discount tiers (not the free tier) may be reduced for assets above statutory exclusions (first $5,000 individual / $8,000 family, home equity, one car, retirement accounts excluded).

CA.summary: California hospitals must have a charity-care and discount-payment policy. Eligible patients at or below 400% FPL pay no more than the hospital's expected Medicare or Medi-Cal rate, whichever is greater.
CA.who: Uninsured patients, or insured patients with "high medical costs" (out-of-pocket at the hospital over 10% of family income), at or below 400% FPL.
CA.hospitalsCovered: General acute, acute psychiatric and special hospitals (not state, DDS or CDCR facilities). Rural hospitals may set a lower threshold.
CA.citation: Cal. Health & Safety Code §§127400, 127405 (amended by AB 2297, eff. 2025-01-01)
caveats: Assets cannot be considered at all when deciding eligibility.
No time limit may be imposed on when you apply.
Emergency physicians must also discount at ≤400% FPL.

NY.summary: New York hospitals must fully waive charges below 200% FPL for uninsured and underinsured patients, and cap payment at 10% (200-300% FPL) or 20% (301-400% FPL) of what Medicaid would have paid, or of insurance cost-sharing.
NY.who: Uninsured patients up to 400% FPL; underinsured patients up to 400% FPL (out-of-pocket over 10% of gross income in the past year); patients who exhausted benefits.
NY.hospitalsCovered: All DOH-licensed hospitals, whether or not they participate in the Indigent Care Pool.
caveats: Verified against DOH agency pages and letters; the statute text itself could not be fetched directly.
Under the 2024 rules: assets can't be considered, you can apply any time (including during collections), and no lawsuit is allowed against patients under 400% FPL.
Payment plans are capped at 5% of gross monthly income; interest capped at 2%.
Q1 (2026-10-02): the cited DOH page does not state the 200%/10%/20% tiers; marked not verified until PHL §2807-k(9-a) itself is fetched.

IL.summary: Illinois urban hospitals must give a 100% discount at or below 200% FPL and some discount up to 600% FPL; rural and Critical Access Hospitals use lower numbers (100% at ≤125% FPL, discount to 300%). An overall cap limits collection to 20% of family income in any 12 months.
IL.who: Uninsured Illinois residents only (intend to live in-state; high-deductible plans count as insured).
IL.hospitalsCovered: All hospitals licensed under the Hospital Licensing Act, plus University of Illinois hospitals. Thresholds differ for rural / Critical Access Hospitals.
caveats: Rural and Critical Access Hospitals use lower thresholds: free ≤125% FPL, discount to 300% FPL only — ask which category your hospital is in.
The discount is defined so the hospital collects at most about 135% of its own cost, not of billed charges.
A 20%-of-income collection cap applies overall; hospitals may opt out above 600% FPL (or 300% FPL for CAH/non-metro) if the patient's assets are high enough.

MD.summary: Maryland hospitals must give free care at or below 200% FPL, reduced-cost care (at least 75%/60% off) from 201-300% FPL, and additional "financial hardship" discounts up to 500% FPL when medical debt exceeds 25% of family income.
MD.who: Patients who lack coverage, or whose coverage doesn't pay the full bill — insured patients are covered too.
MD.hospitalsCovered: Every acute-care and chronic-care hospital under HSCRC jurisdiction.
caveats: The 301-500% FPL "financial hardship" tier only applies if medical debt is over 25% of family income in 12 months — it isn't automatic.
Presumptive free-care eligibility if your household is already in a means-tested program (e.g., free/reduced school meals).
The HSCRC may set even more generous thresholds than the statutory minimums above.

NJ.summary: New Jersey charity care fully covers NJ residents at or below 200% FPL and phases down through 300% FPL. Separately, any uninsured NJ resident under 500% FPL can't be charged more than 115% of the Medicare rate.
NJ.who: Charity care: NJ residents with no coverage, or coverage that pays only part of the bill, not eligible for Medicaid. The 115% cap: any uninsured NJ resident under 500% FPL.
NJ.hospitalsCovered: Charity care: all NJ acute-care hospitals. The 115% cap: all DOH-licensed hospitals.
caveats: Requires New Jersey residency and proof you were screened for other coverage first.
Physician, anesthesiology and similar professional fees are generally not covered by charity care, only facility charges.
Asset limits apply to charity care: $7,500 individual / $15,000 family (spend-down allowed).

CO.summary: Colorado doesn't set a free tier, but caps what hospitals can charge patients at or below 250% FPL to the greater of the Medicare or Medicaid rate — whether or not you have insurance.
CO.who: Uninsured patients must be screened (or formally decline). Insured patients can qualify too. Generally Colorado residents; lawful immigration status is not required.
CO.hospitalsCovered: General acute hospitals, critical access hospitals, freestanding EDs, and licensed professionals billing in those settings.
caveats: Verified against HCPF agency pages; the C.R.S. statute text itself could not be fetched.
Payment plans are capped at 4% of monthly household income for facility bills, 2% for each professional's bill.
A documented decline-to-be-screened form is a complete defense for the hospital — so it's worth actually completing the screening.

OR.summary: Oregon nonprofit hospitals must fully adjust (effectively waive) charges at or below 200% FPL, with discounts of at least 75%, 50% and 25% stepping down through 400% FPL.
OR.who: The free/discount tiers (§442.614) aren't limited to the uninsured on the statute's face. Presumptive screening (§442.615) is required for uninsured patients, Medicaid enrollees, or anyone owing more than $500.
OR.hospitalsCovered: Nonprofit hospitals and their nonprofit affiliated clinics (discount tiers); every hospital licensed under ORS 441.025 (screening duty).
caveats: A hospital may not require a Medicaid application before screening you for charity care.
Presumptive screening needs no documentation and must not affect your credit.
You can apply for assistance up to 12 months after you've already paid.

CT.summary: Connecticut caps what an uninsured patient at or below 250% FPL can be charged at the hospital's own cost of providing the service (its published charges × its cost-to-charge ratio) — but only after a Medicaid denial.
CT.who: Uninsured only. You must have applied for and been denied Medicaid, and have no other coverage.
CT.hospitalsCovered: Hospitals as defined in C.G.S. §19a-490, plus entities they own or are affiliated with.
caveats: This is a cost cap, not free care — you can still owe the hospital's cost of providing the service.
You must apply for and be denied Medicaid first.

MA.summary: Massachusetts runs the Health Safety Net, a state-funded pool hospitals bill into. Per secondary sources, "Low Income Patient" status (about ≤150% FPL) gets full coverage with no deductible, and 150-300% FPL gets partial coverage with a deductible.
MA.who: Unverified: Massachusetts residents only; insured patients are covered via "HSN — Secondary."
MA.hospitalsCovered: Unverified: acute hospitals and community health centers bill the Health Safety Net; it is a state pool, not a hospital-funded discount mandate.
caveats: UNVERIFIED — the official mass.gov regulation pages returned 403 to automated fetching; these numbers come from search-result snippets only, not the regulation text.
This is a state-funded pool billed by the hospital, not a hospital-funded discount like most other states on this list.
Ask the hospital directly about Health Safety Net / Medical Hardship enrollment.

RI.summary: Rhode Island hospitals must give full charity care at or below 200% FPL, and at least some discount — on a scale each hospital sets — from 200-300% FPL.
RI.who: Low-income, uninsured Rhode Island residents ineligible for state, federal or employer coverage.
caveats: Hospitals set their own 200-300% FPL discount scale; they may be more generous but not stricter than the floor.
The hospital must decide within 14 days of a complete application.

NV.summary: Nevada doesn't set an income-based threshold. Instead, "major hospitals" must discount total billed charges by at least 30% for uninsured inpatients who make reasonable payment arrangements within 30 days of notice — regardless of income.
NV.who: Uninsured inpatients not eligible for public programs.
NV.hospitalsCovered: "Major hospitals" (a defined term in NRS 439B; not every hospital qualifies).
caveats: Not income-based — worth asking regardless of your FPL%.
Applies to inpatient uninsured billing at "major hospitals" only; confirm your hospital qualifies.

ME.summary: Maine hospitals must give free medically-necessary care to Maine residents at or below 150% FPL who have no insurance and aren't eligible for public coverage.
ME.who: Maine residents with no insurance and no public-coverage eligibility.
ME.hospitalsCovered: Every hospital must adopt and follow a free-care policy.
caveats: Uninsured only — and not eligible for Medicaid or other public coverage.
A 2024 bill (LD 1955) that would have raised this to 200% FPL did not become law, per secondary reporting.

NM.summary: New Mexico doesn't mandate a charity-care discount. Instead, for "indigent patients" at or below 200% FPL, charges and medical debt can't be pursued through collection actions at all — and existing collection actions must stop.
NM.who: "Indigent patients" (household income ≤200% FPL, measured with Medicaid methods).
NM.hospitalsCovered: Health care facilities, and some independently billing providers.
NM.citation: Patients' Debt Collection Protection Act, NMSA 1978 §57-32-1 et seq.
caveats: This bars debt collection — it does not require a price discount.
Before billing, uninsured patients must be screened for public coverage, other programs and facility financial assistance first.

DE.summary: Starting 2027-01-01, Delaware hospitals must give full financial assistance at or below 300% FPL, with discounts of at least 75%/50% through 400% FPL. This law is not yet in effect.
DE.who: "Financially qualified patients": Delaware residents under the income threshold. Applies to the patient-responsibility portion, so insured patients are covered too.
DE.hospitalsCovered: Hospitals defined in 16 Del. C. §1001, excluding psychiatric-only, rehab-only and long-term-acute-care hospitals.
caveats: NOT YET IN EFFECT as of 2026-10-01 — the law starts 2027-01-01.
Requires Delaware residency.
Each hospital must also have a medical-hardship policy reaching at least 500% FPL.

MN.summary: Minnesota law requires hospitals to screen uninsured patients for presumptive eligibility and charity care, and to give notice — but it sets no specific income-based discount tiers.
caveats: Confirmed: no FPL-based discount tier in this statute — ask the hospital for its own financial assistance policy.

VA.summary: No statewide FPL-based hospital charity-care mandate was found. Virginia has some state indigent-care program activity, per unverified secondary sources.
caveats: UNVERIFIED — a quick search only, no official source fetched.
Ask the hospital directly for its Financial Assistance Policy.

PA.summary: No statewide FPL-based hospital charity-care mandate was found for Pennsylvania in the time available.
caveats: UNVERIFIED — a quick search only, no official source fetched.
Ask the hospital directly for its Financial Assistance Policy.

TX.summary: No statewide FPL-based hospital discount mandate was confirmed for Texas. Nonprofit hospitals have community-benefit obligations tied to their tax-exempt status, per unverified secondary information.
TX.citation: Health & Safety Code ch. 311 (text not obtained)
caveats: UNVERIFIED — the official statutes.capitol.texas.gov page did not return usable text.
Ask about the hospital's own Financial Assistance Policy, especially at nonprofit hospitals.
